title: Lining up to audition at Cosimo Matassa's studio
summary: King describes the long audition lines of songwriters and singers at G&M Studio.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: When record companies would come from Montana in the 1950s, and people would hear, tell me that story about how people would come to the studio to audition. What the audition process was?

Well, both the songwriters and the singers, they had to get in line out there at G&M Studios, which were owned by Cosmo. Cosmo Matias. Cosmo Matias. Cosmo Matias. And they were getting in line. It could be raining. You think they're looking at a gong to wind or something out there. That could be songwriters and artists trying to say, hey, they're getting in line to audition. And they got this guy and they're standing up saying, okay, sing something. And you sing about one, two, three balls. And you know, next, what else you got? And keep the tempo on you like that. Okay, next. And you sing a little bit. Okay, stand over there, that's all. Next fella, set up, bop. And that go on all day like that for about eight hours. And you say, oh God, I think you get up there in front of this guy. Yeah, boy, I need this wild fight, stand over there. No finesse or nothing, just bang. So you know, like you're getting ready to auction that cattle off and stuff and you're scared, your heart beating on you. You know, this. But that's the way the ball was running. You had the people in anticipation, you know, they had, I've heard from my own point of view, I've heard good, for good material, good people, people that could really sing it, it's something to say, it would disqualify it, you know, because they didn't fit within that commercial fast buck thing that they wanted to do with the R&B singing. That was it.
